title: What is known about 1RB0LD_1RC1RF_1LA0RA_0LA0LE_1LD1LA_0RB---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LD_1RC1RF_1LA0RA_0LA0LE_1LD1LA_0RB---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and reduced in Lean to a Collatz-like orbit. The machine follows (Lean, kernel) the map (3k, y) → (4k+1, y+4), (3k+1, y) → (4k+5, y+6), (3k+2, y) → (4k+8, y−1) on its walls, and never halts as long as that orbit, started at (0, 0), never reaches y = 0 with z not a multiple of 3 (not_halts_of_orbit). With native_decide: the first 10,000 macro steps stay inside the rules, so no halt in the first 102400 steps. In Python the orbit ran 106 macro steps (z has 124,940 digits) and y only grew, to 2,999,377; it never came below 4. The counter y behaves like a random walk with drift +3 per step, so an exit looks hopeless, but proving that is a Collatz-type problem, like bbchallenge's Antihydra.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: The cell rules
claims.text: One sweep A>0 (10)^x 0 10 0^(z+3) → A>0 (10)^(x+2) 0 10 0^z in 4x + 11 steps, for every x, z and every tape to the right; and the six ends of a wall (z = 0, 1, 2 left, x = 0 or x ≥ 1), for every x and y. Written by bbtools.symtm.prove.

claims.title: The macro rules
claims.text: With the wall C z y = A>0 0 10 0^z (10)^y 0 1: k sweeps at once (sweeps, cost 4k² + 7k from x = 0), and the three ends end0: S x 0 (y) → C (2x+1) (y+4), end1: S x 1 (y+1) → C (2x+5) (y+7), end2: S x 2 (y+1) → C (2x+8) y.

claims.title: The machine follows the map on (z, y)
claims.text: next z y: (3k, y) → (4k+1, y+4); (3k+1, y) → (4k+5, y+6); (3k+2, y) → (4k+8, y−1), the last two for y ≥ 1. next_sound: the machine goes from C z y to the next wall in exactly mcost z y steps. From blank tape the first wall C 0 0 comes after 7 steps (init_wall).

claims.title: Non-halting reduced to the orbit
claims.text: If the orbit of (0, 0) under next never leaves the rules, the machine never halts from blank tape; and the orbit can leave them only at y = 0 with z not a multiple of 3.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>2400</sup> steps
claims.text: The orbit with its step counts, evaluated by compiled code for 10,000 macro steps (proved to be a run of the machine, orbT_sound, kernel): it stays inside the rules and takes more than 102400 steps.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: The map agrees with the machine
claims.text: py/check.py 1e9 runs the machine 109 steps and finds every wall at the step and with the tape that the map predicts, and no other wall.

claims.title: 10<sup>6</sup> macro steps of the orbit
claims.text: py/orbit.py 1e6: no exit; after 106 steps y = 2,999,377 and z has 124,940 decimal digits; y never fell below 4 after the first step; the three residues of z mod 3 came 332,673 / 333,716 / 333,611 times.

claims.title: Why an exit looks hopeless
claims.text: If z mod 3 behaves like a fair die, y is a random walk with steps +4, +6, −1 (drift +3). From height y it ever reaches 0 with probability about 0.335y; y is 2,999,377 after 106 steps and was never below 4. Every exit would still have to halt from C z 0, which only some do (C 92 0 halts after 54,805 steps; C 8 0 does not in 106).

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.5). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).

claims.title: Does the orbit ever exit?
claims.text: Not known: whether the orbit of (0, 0) ever has y = 0 with z not a multiple of 3 is a Collatz-type question about the digits of z in base 3, like Antihydra.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0LB_1LC0RE_1LA1LD_0LC---_0RB0RF_1RE1RB up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but it comes down to a Collatz-like map. The tape is a wall of 0s that the head eats three cells per sweep; when the wall is used up it is rebuilt about 4/3 as long, and a counter y moves by +4, +6 or −1 depending on the wall's length mod 3. Lean proves the machine never halts unless y ever hits 0. In a million rebuilds y has only climbed, to almost three million.

facts.text: The machine follows this map; it halts only if y reaches 0 (Lean, kernel).
No halt, proved in Lean by running 10,000 macro steps.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.5). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 44,644 cells (32,717 left of the start, 176 right), with a density of 1s of 0.322.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: What the tape is made of
html: All the action is on the left: the right end of the tape never moves after the first few hundred steps. Look at the tape whenever the head, in state A, stands on the leftmost cell it has ever visited, with nothing grown yet. It is always the same shape, which we call a wall C z y:

A>0 (10)^x 0 10 0^(z+3) → A>0 (10)^(x+2) 0 10 0^z in 4x + 11 steps (sweep). The sweep never looks at the 10s on the right. So a wall of z = 3k + r zeros takes k sweeps, 4k² + 7k steps, and leaves r = 0, 1 or 2 zeros and x = 2k grown 10s.

sections.heading: When the wall is gone it is rebuilt longer
html: With fewer than three 0s left, the head turns the 2k grown 10s back into 0s, walks to the right end and back, and a new wall begins: the grown part becomes the new wall, about twice the 2k, and the 10s on the right change by a few, depending on the 0s that were left:

left overnew wallnew ystepsLean
r = 04k + 1y + 48k + 8y + 37end0
r = 14k + 5y + 616k + 16y + 94end1
r = 24k + 8y − 116k + 28end2
The last two need y ≥ 1 (there must be a 10 on the right to use). So one wall to the next is the map
(3k, y) → (4k+1, y+4)   (3k+1, y) → (4k+5, y+6)   (3k+2, y) → (4k+8, y−1)
proved in Lean for every k and y (next_sound), with the exact step count.

sections.heading: A Collatz-like map with a counter
html: The wall length z is multiplied by about 4/3 at every rebuild, and what happens next depends on z mod 3, that is on the last digit of z in base 3. That is the shape of a Collatz problem: the digits of a number being repeatedly multiplied by 4/3 look random, but nobody can prove anything about them. The counter y is the running score: +4 when the digit is 0, +6 when it is 1, −1 when it is 2. The first walls:

wallzz = 3k + ry
003·0 + 00
113·0 + 14
253·1 + 210
3123·4 + 09
4173·5 + 213
5283·9 + 112
6413·13 + 218
7603·20 + 017
8813·27 + 021
91093·36 + 125
101493·49 + 231
112043·68 + 030
122733·91 + 034
133653·121 + 238

This is the same kind of object as bbchallenge's Antihydra (n → ⌊3n/2⌋, a counter +2 on even, −1 on odd), with 4/3 in place of 3/2 and a much stronger upward drift: on average y gains (4 + 6 − 1)/3 = 3 per step. In 106 steps (Python, py/orbit.py; z then has 124,940 digits) the three digits came 332,673 / 333,716 / 333,611 times and y reached 2,999,377, never dropping below 4 after the first step.

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html: The machine halts on F reading a 1. Inside the walls that never happens. It could only happen after the map breaks down: a wall with y = 0 (no 10s left on the right) and z not a multiple of 3. Then the head uses up the final 0 1 and the tape takes another shape; from such a configuration the machine sometimes halts (from C 92 0 after 54,805 steps) and sometimes not (from C 8 0, no halt in 106 steps).

Lean proves (not_halts_of_orbit, orb_exit): if the orbit of (0, 0) never reaches y = 0 with z not divisible by 3, the machine never halts. y can only go down one step at a time, by the digit 2, so it would need a run of about y more 2s than 0s and 1s. If the digits are like dice, the chance of ever getting from height y down to 0 is about 0.335y: after a million steps, about 10−1,400,000. Turning “like dice” into a proof is the open Collatz-type problem.

sections.heading: What is proved
html: Lean, kernel: the sweep and the six ways a wall ends, for all values (lean/Rules.lean, written by bbtools.symtm, and lean/Macro.lean); the map next with its step count and that the machine follows it (next_sound); the first wall after 7 steps; and the reduction not_halts_of_orbit (lean/Reduce.lean).
Lean, native_decide (lean/OrbitRun.lean): the first 10,000 macro steps stay inside the rules, more than 102400 machine steps.
Computed: the map checked against the machine at every wall of the first 109 steps (py/check.py); 106 macro steps of the orbit (py/orbit.py).
Open: whether the orbit ever exits.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: A wall of 0s is eaten three cells per sweep while a block of 10s grows by two; each wall maps (3k+r, y) to (4k+c, y+d) with (c, d) = (1, +4), (5, +6), (8, −1), a Collatz-like map whose counter y drifts upward; proved in Lean that it never halts unless y ever reaches 0 at a z not divisible by 3.
